## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- describe the **toolchain** that turns C and C++ source code into a running
  program — preprocessor, compiler, assembler, linker, loader — and the file
  each stage produces;
- install a compiler and a debugger on **Linux** and on **Windows** (GCC via
  MSYS2, or Microsoft's MSVC), and configure **Visual Studio Code** to build,
  run and debug C and C++ programs;
- compile from the command line with the right **flags** (language standard,
  warnings, optimisation, debug information, sanitizers) and read compiler
  **diagnostics**;
- split a program into **header** and **source** files and build it with
  **Make** or **CMake**;
- **prove** which files must be recompiled after a change, and why Make's
  timestamp rule gets it right.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
Preparing a workstation to write, compile, run and debug C and C++ programs
with Visual Studio Code, on Windows and on Linux.
:::

## Intuition: a translator, not a reader

In Part I, Python read your program and carried it out line by line, a bit
like a cook who reads a recipe aloud while cooking (@sec-python-language). C
and C++ work differently: before anything runs, a **translator** rewrites the
whole recipe into the cook's native language — the machine code of your
processor (@sec-von-neumann) — and binds it into a booklet, the
**executable**. Running the program means handing the booklet to the cook.

This has three consequences you will feel from day one:

1. there is a **build step** between editing and running: forget it and you
   run yesterday's program;
2. many mistakes are caught **before** the program runs, by the translator —
   and the error messages refer to a moment ("compile time") different from
   the one in which the program misbehaves ("run time");
3. the executable is tied to a **platform** (processor + operating system):
   the booklet written for one cook is unreadable to another.

Chapter [-@sec-ch-compiled] studies these trade-offs in depth. This chapter is
practical: we set up the tools, follow a program through the translator, and
learn to drive a debugger.

## The toolchain: from source to process {#sec-toolchain}

A **toolchain** is the chain of programs that turns source files into a
running process. For C and C++ the stages are always the same, whatever the
compiler brand [@bryant2016, ch. 1 and 7; @levine1999]:

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-cap: "The C/C++ toolchain. The compiler driver (`gcc`, `g++`, `clang++`, `cl`) runs the first four stages for you; the loader is part of the operating system."
flowchart LR
    A["hello.cpp<br/>source"] -->|preprocessor| B["hello.ii<br/>pure C++"]
    B -->|compiler| C["hello.s<br/>assembly"]
    C -->|assembler| D["hello.o<br/>object file"]
    D -->|linker| E["hello<br/>executable"]
    L["libstdc++, libc<br/>libraries"] -->|linker| E
    E -->|loader| F["process<br/>in memory"]
```

| Stage | Input → output | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **preprocessor** | `.c`/`.cpp` → translation unit | executes the `#` directives: pastes the text of `#include`d headers, expands `#define` macros, keeps or drops `#if` blocks |
| **compiler proper** | translation unit → assembly (`.s`) | parses, type-checks, optimises, and emits instructions for the target processor |
| **assembler** | `.s` → object file (`.o`, `.obj`) | encodes the instructions in binary; leaves **symbols** (names of functions and variables defined elsewhere) unresolved |
| **linker** | object files + libraries → executable | resolves every symbol to an address and lays out the final file (ELF on Linux, PE on Windows, Mach-O on macOS) |
| **loader** | executable → process | the operating system maps the file into memory, loads shared libraries, and jumps to the entry point, which eventually calls `main` |

: The stages of the toolchain {#tbl-toolchain}

The command `g++ hello.cpp -o hello` runs the first four stages in one go:
`g++` is a **driver** that calls the real tools for you. Options let us stop
after any stage, so we can look at each intermediate product. Here is the
program we will follow:

```{python}
show(r"""
// hello.cpp — the classic first program, plus one function of our own
#include <iostream>     // preprocessor: paste the declarations of the I/O library

int square(int x) {     // a function we define in this translation unit
    return x * x;
}

int main() {            // execution starts here
    std::cout << "Hello, C++! 7 squared is " << square(7) << '\n';
    return 0;           // 0 = success, reported to the operating system
}
""", name="hello.cpp")
```

### Stage 1: the preprocessor

`g++ -E` stops after preprocessing. The single line `#include <iostream>` is
replaced by the full text of the header and of every header it includes in
turn:

```{python}
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -E hello.cpp -o hello.ii && wc -l hello.cpp hello.ii")
```

Our 11-line file has become a translation unit of tens of thousands of lines
— and **every** source file that includes `<iostream>` pays that price again.
This is why large C++ projects compile slowly, and why C++20 introduced
**modules** (`import std;` in C++23), which are compiled once and reused
[@stroustrup2022, §3.2.2].

### Stage 2: the compiler proper

`g++ -S` stops after compilation and leaves human-readable **assembly**. Let
us look at the instructions generated for `square`, with optimisations on
(`-O2`):

```{python}
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -S hello.cpp -o hello.s && "
   "sed -n '/^_Z6squarei:/,/ret/p' hello.s | grep -v '^\\s*\\.cfi'")
```

Apart from a label and `endbr64` (a marker used by the processor's
control-flow protection), the function is three instructions, written in the
AT&T syntax *operation source, destination*: multiply the argument by itself
(`edi` is the register in which the x86-64 calling convention passes the first
integer argument), copy the result into `eax` (the register that holds the
return value), return. The odd name `_Z6squarei` is
the **mangled** name of `square(int)`: C++ encodes the parameter types in the
symbol name so that overloaded functions (@sec-ch-c-vs-cpp) get distinct
symbols.

### Stage 3: the assembler and the symbol table

`g++ -c` produces an **object file**. `nm` lists its **symbols**: `T` marks a
function defined here (in the *text* section), `U` a symbol that is **used but
undefined** — the linker will have to find it elsewhere.

```{python}
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -c hello.cpp -o hello.o && nm -C hello.o | grep -E ' (T|U) '",
   max_lines=12)
```

`square` and `main` are defined here; the stream `std::cout`, the output
operators and the support routines come from the C++ standard library
(`libstdc++` for GCC).

### Stage 4: the linker

Linking connects the `U`s to their definitions and produces the executable:

```{python}
sh("g++ hello.o -o hello && ./hello && echo \"exit status: $?\"")
```

`$?` is the shell's variable holding the **exit status** of the last command:
the `return 0` of `main` reached the operating system. We will use exit
statuses to make C++ and Python programs cooperate in @sec-ch-cpp-python.

::: {#exm-link-error}
## A link error is not a compile error
If a function is **declared** (its signature is known) but never **defined**
(its body is missing), every translation unit compiles, and the error appears
only at link time:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
int cube(int x);                          // declaration only: "trust me, it exists"
int main() { std::cout << cube(3) << '\n'; }
""", name="nodef.cpp", expect_error=True)
```

The linker, not the compiler, complains: `undefined reference to cube(int)`.
Learning to tell **which tool** produced an error message is the first step to
fixing it.
:::

## Compilers, standards and versions {#sec-compilers}

### The three major compilers

- **GCC**, the GNU Compiler Collection, started by Richard Stallman in 1987;
  the default compiler on Linux. Drivers: `gcc` for C, `g++` for C++
  [@gccmanual].
- **Clang**, the C/C++ front end of the **LLVM** project, started by Chris
  Lattner at the University of Illinois [@lattner2004]; the default on macOS
  and widely used on Linux and Windows. Drivers: `clang`, `clang++`.
- **MSVC**, Microsoft's C/C++ compiler, shipped with Visual Studio; driver
  `cl.exe`, Windows only.

All three implement the same **ISO standards**, with small differences in
extensions, diagnostics and the date at which they support new features. At
the time of writing (November 2026) the latest major releases are GCC 16.1
(April 2026), which made C++20 the default C++ dialect, and LLVM/Clang 23.1
(August 2026) [@gcc16; @llvm23].

### The language standards

C and C++ are defined by international standards maintained by two ISO
working groups: WG14 (C) and WG21 (C++). A program written against a standard
works with any conforming compiler — this is the basis of the portability we
discuss in @sec-ch-compiled.

| Language | Standard | Informal name | Highlights |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | ANSI X3.159-1989 / ISO 9899:1990 | C89/C90 | the language of K&R 2nd edition [@kernighan1988] |
| C | ISO/IEC 9899:1999 | C99 | `//` comments, `<stdbool.h>`, `<stdint.h>`, declarations anywhere |
| C | ISO/IEC 9899:2011 / 2018 | C11 / C17 | threads, atomics, `_Static_assert`; C17 is a bug-fix release |
| C | ISO/IEC 9899:2024 | C23 | `bool`, `true`, `false` and `nullptr` as keywords, `constexpr` objects [@iso9899c23] |
| C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:1998 / 2003 | C++98/03 | the first standard: templates, the STL, exceptions |
| C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:2011 | C++11 | move semantics, `auto`, lambdas, smart pointers: "modern C++" |
| C++ | 2014, 2017 | C++14, C++17 | refinements; `std::optional`, `std::string_view`, structured bindings |
| C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:2020 | C++20 | concepts, ranges, modules, coroutines, `<=>` |
| C++ | ISO/IEC 14882:2024 | C++23 | `import std;`, `std::print`, `std::expected` [@iso14882] |

: The C and C++ standards {#tbl-standards}

C++26 completed its technical work in March 2026, but in October 2026 its
international approval ballot did not pass, mainly over the new *contracts*
feature; at the time of writing the committee is deciding how to proceed
[@sutter2026]. Nothing in this part depends on C++26.

::: {.callout-important}
## The toolchain used in this book
Every C++ example in this part is compiled with **GCC (`g++`) using
`-std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -Wextra`** and every C example with **`gcc -std=c17`**,
on x86-64 Linux, and actually executed when the book is built: the outputs you
see are real. Where a result depends on the platform (sizes of types, timings),
the text says so.
:::

```{python}
sh("g++ --version | head -1 && gcc --version | head -1")
```

## Installing the tools {#sec-installing}

### On Linux

Linux distributions package GCC, the GNU debugger GDB, Make and CMake. On
Debian and Ubuntu:

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential gdb cmake   # gcc, g++, make, libc headers, gdb, cmake
g++ --version                                # check
```

(On Fedora: `sudo dnf install gcc-c++ gdb make cmake`.) Clang is one command
away (`sudo apt install clang`), and having two compilers is useful: a program
that compiles cleanly with both is more likely to be standard-conforming.

### On Windows

Windows does not ship a C++ compiler. Three good options:

1. **GCC through MSYS2** (the route of the VS Code documentation
   [@vscodecpp]). Install MSYS2 from its web site, open the *MSYS2 UCRT64*
   terminal and install the toolchain with
   `pacman -S --needed base-devel mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-toolchain`; then add
   `C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin` to the Windows `PATH` environment variable, open a
   **new** terminal and check `g++ --version` and `gdb --version`. You get the
   same compiler used in this book, producing native Windows executables
   (`.exe`).
2. **MSVC**, by installing *Visual Studio* or the lighter *Build Tools for
   Visual Studio* with the "Desktop development with C++" workload. Compile
   from the *Developer Command Prompt* with
   `cl /std:c++20 /EHsc /W4 hello.cpp`.
3. **WSL** (Windows Subsystem for Linux): a real Linux distribution inside
   Windows; then follow the Linux instructions. VS Code connects to it
   transparently.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The most common installation problem
`'g++' is not recognized as an internal or external command`: the compiler is
installed but its folder is not in `PATH`, or the terminal was opened **before**
`PATH` was changed. Close every terminal (and VS Code), reopen, and run
`where g++` (Windows) or `which g++` (Linux) to see which compiler, if any, is
found.
:::

### Visual Studio Code

VS Code is an **editor**, not a compiler: it calls the compiler you installed.
Install VS Code and, from the Extensions view, Microsoft's **C/C++** extension
(`ms-vscode.cpptools`), which adds code completion (IntelliSense), build tasks
and debugging. When you first run *Run C/C++ File* on an open source file, VS
Code asks which compiler to use and writes its configuration in a `.vscode`
folder of your project:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `tasks.json` | how to **build**: the compiler command and its arguments |
| `launch.json` | how to **run and debug**: which executable, which debugger (`gdb`, `lldb` or the MSVC debugger) |
| `c_cpp_properties.json` | how IntelliSense should **understand** the code: compiler path, standard, include folders |

: The VS Code configuration files {#tbl-vscode-files}

The default build task compiles the *active file* only, with debug information
and no warnings. It is worth editing `tasks.json` once to use the flags of the
next section. A version that works on Linux and, with `g++.exe`, on Windows:

```json
{
  "version": "2.0.0",
  "tasks": [
    {
      "type": "cppbuild",
      "label": "C/C++: g++ build active file",
      "command": "g++",
      "args": [
        "-std=c++20", "-Wall", "-Wextra", "-Wpedantic",
        "-g", "-O0",
        "${file}",
        "-o", "${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension}"
      ],
      "problemMatcher": ["$gcc"],
      "group": { "kind": "build", "isDefault": true }
    }
  ]
}
```

The `problemMatcher` turns the compiler's diagnostics into clickable entries in
the *Problems* panel. For projects with several files, prefer a build system
(@sec-build-systems): VS Code's *CMake Tools* extension drives CMake directly.

## Compiler flags that matter {#sec-flags}

A compiler has hundreds of options; a handful matter every day.

| Flag (GCC/Clang) | MSVC | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `-std=c++20`, `-std=c17` | `/std:c++20` | which **language standard** to accept |
| `-Wall -Wextra` | `/W4` | enable the most useful **warnings** |
| `-Wpedantic` | `/permissive-` | reject non-standard extensions |
| `-Werror` | `/WX` | treat warnings as errors |
| `-O0`, `-O2`, `-O3` | `/Od`, `/O2` | **optimisation** level: none (best for debugging) to aggressive |
| `-g` | `/Zi` | include **debug information** (source lines, variable names) |
| `-fsanitize=address,undefined` | `/fsanitize=address` | add run-time checks for memory errors and undefined behaviour |
| `-o name` | `/Fe:name` | name of the output file |

: Everyday compiler flags {#tbl-flags}

### Warnings are free bug reports

A **warning** is the compiler saying: "this is legal, but it is very probably
not what you meant." Here are three classic mistakes that compile — and that
`-Wall -Wextra` points out:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int n;                              // (1) never initialised
    unsigned limit = 10;
    for (int i = 0; i < limit; ++i) {   // (2) signed/unsigned comparison
        if (i = 5)                      // (3) assignment, not comparison!
            std::cout << "five\n";
    }
    std::cout << n << '\n';
}
""", name="warnings.cpp", flags=("-O2", "-Wall", "-Wextra"), run_it=False)
```

Mistake (3) would make the loop print `five` forever, since `i = 5` sets `i`
and evaluates to 5, which is true; mistake (1) prints an unpredictable value.
**Compile with warnings on, and treat every warning as an error until you can
explain why it is harmless.**

### Sanitizers: run-time checks for free

Some errors cannot be detected at compile time. The **sanitizers** of GCC and
Clang instrument the program with checks: AddressSanitizer detects
out-of-bounds accesses, use of freed memory and leaks, with a typical slowdown
of about 2× [@serebryany2012]; UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer detects, for
example, signed integer overflow. Without the sanitizer this program silently
writes past the end of an array; with it, it stops at the faulty line:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a[4] = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= 4; ++i)     // off by one: a[4] does not exist
        sum += a[i];
    std::cout << sum << '\n';
}
""", name="oob.cpp", sanitize="address", flags=("-O0",), filter_lines=sanitizer_summary)
```

(We show only the key lines of the report; the full report also maps the
memory around the bad address.) Read it from the top: the kind of error
(`stack-buffer-overflow`), the access (`READ of size 4`), and the first frame
of the stack trace, `in main oob.cpp:7` — file and line. Sanitizers are available on Linux and macOS
with GCC and Clang; MSVC supports AddressSanitizer with `/fsanitize=address`.
We will use them throughout this part, in particular for the memory errors of
@sec-ch-c-intro and @sec-ch-c-vs-cpp.

## Debugging {#sec-debugging}

A **debugger** runs your program under control: it can stop it at a
**breakpoint**, execute it **one line at a time**, and show the values of
variables and the **call stack** (the chain of function calls that led to the
current line, @sec-recursion). In VS Code you click in the margin to set a
breakpoint and press <kbd>F5</kbd>; underneath, VS Code talks to GDB (or LLDB,
or the MSVC debugger). We can drive GDB directly to see what happens. Compile
with `-g -O0` (debug information, no optimisation, so that the machine code
follows the source line by line):

```{python}
show(r"""
#include <iostream>

int square(int x) {
    int r = x * x;
    return r;
}

int main() {
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; ++i)
        total += square(i);
    std::cout << total << '\n';
}
""", name="debugme.cpp")
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -g -O0 debugme.cpp -o debugme && "
   "gdb -batch -q -ex 'break square' -ex run -ex backtrace -ex 'info args' "
   "-ex finish -ex 'print total' ./debugme",
   filter_fn=lambda l: "libthread_db" not in l and l.strip())
```

| What you want | GDB command | VS Code |
|---|---|---|
| stop at a line or function | `break square`, `break debugme.cpp:11` | click in the margin |
| start / continue | `run` / `continue` | <kbd>F5</kbd> |
| next line (over calls) | `next` | <kbd>F10</kbd> |
| enter the called function | `step` | <kbd>F11</kbd> |
| run to the end of this function | `finish` | <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F11</kbd> |
| show the call stack | `backtrace` | *Call Stack* panel |
| show a variable | `print total`, `info locals` | *Variables* / *Watch* panels |

: Debugger commands and their VS Code equivalents {#tbl-gdb}

Note the last line of the session: after `finish`, `total` is still `0`.
Execution stopped in the middle of line 11, *after* `square(1)` returned
(`Value returned is $1 = 1`) but *before* the addition — the debugger shows the
state of the machine at an exact instant, which is what makes it so precise.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A debugging method
A debugger is not a substitute for thinking. Kernighan and Pike's advice
[@kernighan1999, ch. 5] still holds: **reproduce** the failure with the
smallest input, **form a hypothesis** about the cause, **test** it (with a
breakpoint, a `print`, an assertion), and only then change the code.
:::

## Programs in several files {#sec-multifile}

Real programs are split into files, for the same reasons as Python modules
(@sec-modularity): each file has one responsibility, can be understood alone,
and — specific to compiled languages — can be **compiled separately**.

### Declarations and definitions

C and C++ distinguish two things that Python merges:

- a **declaration** introduces a name and its type: `int square(int x);`
  ("a function `square` exists, taking an `int` and returning an `int`");
- a **definition** also provides the body (or, for a variable, the storage).

A name must be **declared before it is used** in each translation unit, and
**defined exactly once** in the whole program — the **one-definition rule**
(ODR) [@iso14882, §basic.def.odr]. The convention that follows is:

- a **header file** (`.h`, `.hpp`) contains declarations — the **interface**;
- a **source file** (`.c`, `.cpp`) contains the definitions — the
  **implementation**;
- every file that needs the interface `#include`s the header.

```{python}
show(r"""
// geometry.hpp — interface: what other files may use
#pragma once                       // include this header at most once per translation unit

double circle_area(double radius);
double rectangle_area(double width, double height);
""", name="geometry.hpp")
show(r"""
// geometry.cpp — implementation
#include "geometry.hpp"            // quotes: search the project folder first

constexpr double pi = 3.141592653589793;

double circle_area(double radius) { return pi * radius * radius; }
double rectangle_area(double width, double height) { return width * height; }
""", name="geometry.cpp")
show(r"""
// main.cpp — the program
#include <iostream>                // angle brackets: a system header
#include "geometry.hpp"

int main() {
    std::cout << "circle r=1:    " << circle_area(1.0) << '\n'
              << "rectangle 2x3: " << rectangle_area(2.0, 3.0) << '\n';
}
""", name="main.cpp")
```

Each source file is compiled **separately** into an object file, then the
objects are linked:

```{python}
sh("g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -c geometry.cpp && "
   "g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -c main.cpp && "
   "g++ geometry.o main.o -o shapes && ./shapes")
```

`#pragma once` (supported by all major compilers, though not part of the
standard) prevents a header from being pasted twice into the same translation
unit, which would repeat its definitions of types. The portable equivalent is
an **include guard**:

```cpp
#ifndef GEOMETRY_HPP
#define GEOMETRY_HPP
// ... declarations ...
#endif
```

### Build systems: Make and CMake {#sec-build-systems}

Typing the commands above by hand does not scale, and recompiling *every* file
after each change wastes time. A **build system** records how each file is
produced from others and redoes only the necessary work. The classic one is
**Make**, written by Stuart Feldman at Bell Labs in 1976 [@feldman1979]. A
`Makefile` lists **rules**: a *target*, its *prerequisites*, and the commands
that rebuild the target from them.

```{python}
show("""
# Makefile — each rule: target: prerequisites, then commands indented with a TAB
CXX      = g++
CXXFLAGS = -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2

shapes: main.o geometry.o
\t$(CXX) main.o geometry.o -o shapes

main.o: main.cpp geometry.hpp
\t$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -c main.cpp

geometry.o: geometry.cpp geometry.hpp
\t$(CXX) $(CXXFLAGS) -c geometry.cpp

clean:
\trm -f shapes *.o
""", name="Makefile", lang="makefile")
```

Make rebuilds a target when it is **missing** or **older** than one of its
prerequisites. Watch it at work: a full build, then nothing to do, then a
change to `main.cpp` only:

```{python}
sh("rm -f *.o shapes && make && echo '--- second run:' && make && "
   "echo '--- after touching main.cpp:' && touch main.cpp && make")
```

After `main.cpp` changed, only `main.o` and the executable were rebuilt;
`geometry.o` was reused. Why is that exactly the right set? The **dependency
graph** answers.

::: {#def-build-graph}
## Build graph
A **build graph** is a finite directed acyclic graph whose vertices are files
and with an edge $u \to v$ when $v$ is built from $u$ ($u$ is a prerequisite of
$v$). Vertices without incoming edges are **sources** (written by hand); the
others are **targets**, each produced by a deterministic command from its
direct prerequisites.
:::

::: {#prp-rebuild-set}
## What must be rebuilt
If the set $C$ of source files changes, a target must be rebuilt if and only
if it is **reachable** from some file of $C$ (there is a directed path from a
changed file to it). Moreover, rebuilding the reachable targets in a
topological order (@thm-toposort) brings every target up to date with one
command each.
:::

*In one line:* a change propagates exactly along the arrows — what is
downstream of an edited file is stale, everything else can be reused.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-rebuild-set
*Not reachable ⇒ unaffected.* By induction along a topological order: if no
prerequisite of a target $t$ is a changed file or a stale target, then $t$'s
command receives exactly the same inputs as last time and, being
deterministic, produces the same output — so the old $t$ is still correct. A
target not reachable from $C$ has, by definition, no changed or reachable
prerequisite, so the induction applies to it.

*Reachable ⇒ must be rebuilt.* If $t$ is reachable, some path
$c \to v_1 \to \dots \to v_k = t$ starts at a changed file $c$. In general the
new content of $c$ can change $v_1$, which can change $v_2$, and so on; a build
system that does not inspect the *meaning* of the files cannot exclude it, so
it must rebuild $t$. (A smarter system may still discover that a rebuilt file
is byte-identical to the old one and stop the propagation there.)

*Order.* Processing reachable targets in a topological order guarantees that
when $t$ is rebuilt, all its prerequisites are already up to date; hence each
target is built once. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.deep}
## Why Make's timestamp rule implements @prp-rebuild-set
Make does not know which files you changed; it compares **modification
times**. To bring target $t$ up to date it first, recursively, brings every
prerequisite up to date, and then rebuilds $t$ if $t$ is missing or some
prerequisite is newer than $t$. Suppose that after the previous complete build
every target was newer than its prerequisites, and that editing a file sets its
time to "now", later than every existing file. Then, by induction along a
topological order, a target gets a time later than its old one exactly when one
of its prerequisites does — i.e. exactly when it is reachable from an edited
file. The assumptions matter: copying an *old* file over a source (which keeps
the old timestamp), a clock that goes backwards, or a prerequisite missing from
the Makefile (a header not listed!) all break the guarantee. This is why
compilers can **generate** the header dependencies for you (`g++ -MMD`), and
why modern tools such as Ninja and Bazel also compare file contents.
:::

Writing Makefiles by hand is error-prone and not portable to MSVC. Most C++
projects use **CMake**, which *generates* the build files for the platform
(Makefiles, Ninja files, Visual Studio solutions) from a short description:

```{python}
show("""
# CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(shapes LANGUAGES CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)

add_executable(shapes main.cpp geometry.cpp)
target_compile_options(shapes PRIVATE
    $<$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>:/W4>
    $<$<NOT:$<CXX_COMPILER_ID:MSVC>>:-Wall -Wextra>)
""", name="CMakeLists.txt", lang="cmake")
sh("cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja > /dev/null && cmake --build build && ./build/shapes")
```

The two commands are the same on every platform: `cmake -S . -B build`
(configure: generate the build files in a separate `build` folder) and
`cmake --build build` (build). CMake works out the header dependencies by
itself. We will use this setup for the project (@sec-ch-project-crm).

## Reading compiler errors {#sec-reading-errors}

C++ error messages have a reputation for being long. Three rules make them
manageable:

1. **Fix the first error first.** Later errors are often consequences of the
   first (a missing `;` can confuse the parser for many lines).
2. **Find `file:line:column`.** Every diagnostic starts with a location; the
   text after `error:` is the message, and `note:` lines add context.
3. **Identify the tool.** A message mentioning `undefined reference` comes from
   the linker (@exm-link-error); everything else from the compiler.

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string name = "Ada";
    int length = name.size()       // missing semicolon
    std::cout << nmae << '\n';     // misspelt name
}
""", name="errors.cpp", expect_error=True)
```

GCC reports the missing semicolon — at the place where it noticed it, the
beginning of the *next* line, since only there does the statement become
impossible — and says nothing about the misspelt name: after the first error it
skipped the rest of that statement. Add the semicolon and compile again; now the
second mistake surfaces, with a suggestion:

```{python}
run(r"""
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::string name = "Ada";
    auto length = name.size();
    std::cout << nmae << ' ' << length << '\n';
}
""", name="errors2.cpp", expect_error=True)
```

This is rule 1 in action: one real mistake can hide or cause others, so fix the
first one and recompile.

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The CRM of @sec-ch-project-crm is a multi-file C++
program: one header and one source file per component, a small `main.cpp`, and a
`CMakeLists.txt` (requirement R12, @sec-crm-brief). It is built with the flags
of @tbl-flags — warnings on, and sanitizers during development — and its README
gives the two CMake commands of @sec-build-systems, which work unchanged on
Linux and on Windows.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Running a stale executable.** You edited the source but did not rebuild: in
  a compiled language, *save* is not *build*.
- **Compiler not in `PATH`** after installation; reopen the terminal and VS
  Code.
- **Ignoring warnings.** Most beginners' bugs (uninitialised variables, `=`
  instead of `==`, signed/unsigned comparisons) are reported as warnings.
- **Debugging optimised code.** With `-O2` the debugger may skip lines or show
  variables as `<optimized out>`: debug with `-O0 -g`.
- **Definitions in headers.** A function *defined* (not just declared) in a
  header included by two source files breaks the one-definition rule:
  `multiple definition of …` at link time (unless it is `inline`).
- **Headers missing from the Makefile** dependencies: Make does not rebuild
  what it does not know about. Use CMake, or `-MMD`.
:::

## Summary

- The **toolchain** turns sources into a process in stages: preprocessor →
  compiler → assembler → linker → loader. `-E`, `-S`, `-c` stop after each
  stage; `nm` shows the symbols an object file defines and needs.
- **GCC**, **Clang** and **MSVC** implement the ISO **C** and **C++**
  standards; this book uses `g++ -std=c++20` and `gcc -std=c17`.
- On Linux install `build-essential` and `gdb`; on Windows use MSYS2's GCC,
  MSVC, or WSL. VS Code stores build, debug and IntelliSense settings in
  `tasks.json`, `launch.json` and `c_cpp_properties.json`.
- Always compile with **warnings** (`-Wall -Wextra`) and, while developing,
  with **sanitizers**; debug with `-g -O0`.
- **Headers** hold declarations, **sources** definitions (one-definition
  rule). A build system rebuilds exactly the targets **reachable** from the
  changed files (@prp-rebuild-set); **CMake** generates the build files for any
  platform.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-cpp1-stages}
For each message, say which stage of the toolchain produced it and why:
(a) `fatal error: geometri.hpp: No such file or directory`;
(b) `error: 'cout' is not a member of 'std'`;
(c) `undefined reference to 'circle_area(double)'`;
(d) `multiple definition of 'pi'`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) Preprocessor: it could not find the file named in an `#include` (a typo).
(b) Compiler: the name `std::cout` is used but not declared — `<iostream>` was
not included. (c) Linker: `circle_area` was declared but no object file defines
it (e.g. `geometry.cpp` was not compiled or not linked). (d) Linker: two object
files define the same non-`inline` variable, typically because the definition
`double pi = …;` was put in a header included by two sources (one-definition
rule). Fix: declare it `inline constexpr` in the header, or define it in one
source file.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp1-rebuild}
A project has sources `a.hpp`, `a.cpp`, `b.hpp`, `b.cpp`, `main.cpp`, where
`a.cpp` includes `a.hpp`; `b.cpp` includes `b.hpp` and `a.hpp`; `main.cpp`
includes `b.hpp`. Each `.cpp` is compiled to a `.o` and the three objects are
linked into `app`. Draw the build graph. Which targets are rebuilt when
(a) `a.hpp` changes; (b) `b.cpp` changes; (c) `main.cpp` changes?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Edges: `a.hpp → a.o`, `a.cpp → a.o`, `b.hpp → b.o`, `a.hpp → b.o`,
`b.cpp → b.o`, `b.hpp → main.o`, `main.cpp → main.o`, and `a.o`, `b.o`,
`main.o → app`. By @prp-rebuild-set: (a) `a.o`, `b.o`, `app`; (b) `b.o`,
`app`; (c) `main.o`, `app`. Note that in (a) `main.o` is *not* rebuilt, even
though `main.cpp` uses `b.hpp`, because `main.cpp` does not (transitively)
include `a.hpp`.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp1-flags}
Compile the `warnings.cpp` program of @sec-flags with `-Werror` added. What
happens, and why is `-Werror` a good default for your own projects but a bad
idea in code you distribute to others?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Compilation fails: each warning becomes an error, so no executable is produced
until the three problems are fixed. In your own project this forces warnings to
be dealt with immediately. In distributed source code, however, a newer
compiler version may introduce *new* warnings, so users would be unable to
build perfectly correct code with their compiler; enable `-Werror` in your
development and CI builds, not in the default build.
:::

::: {#exr-cpp1-headers}
How many lines does the preprocessed translation unit of a file containing only
`#include <vector>` and `#include <string>` have with your compiler? Estimate
how many lines the compiler must parse in a project of 200 source files that
each include `<iostream>`, `<vector>` and `<string>`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Measure with `g++ -std=c++20 -E file.cpp | wc -l`. With GCC 13 and libstdc++
each of these headers expands to tens of thousands of lines, and together
(their contents overlap) to a few tens of thousands. With $L$ lines per
translation unit and $n = 200$ files, the compiler parses about $nL$ lines —
several million — although the headers are identical every time: the
redundancy that precompiled headers and C++20 modules remove.
:::

- @vscodecpp — the official VS Code tutorials: *GCC on Windows via MinGW*,
  *Microsoft C++ on Windows*, *GCC on Linux*; and the pages on debugging and
  `c_cpp_properties.json`.
- @gccmanual — chapter *GCC Command Options*, in particular *Options to Request
  or Suppress Warnings*, *Options for Debugging* and *Program Instrumentation
  Options* (sanitizers).
- @bryant2016 — ch. 1 (a tour of the toolchain) and ch. 7 (linking: symbols,
  relocation, static and shared libraries).
- @levine1999 — the classic book on linkers and loaders.
- @feldman1979 — the original paper on Make, short and readable.
- @serebryany2012 — how AddressSanitizer works (shadow memory), and its cost.
- @kernighan1999, ch. 5 — debugging strategies that do not depend on the tool.
